Court Chair Voegele ruled the Fiscal Court's 2026-08-24 special-called meeting void because the court failed to approve its own agenda, so the item restarted. On 2026-09-01 the Fiscal Court reconsidered and unanimously adopted substantive revisions to the draft regulations (still numbered KOC 26-920-5): striking all references to 'large'/'hyperscale' data centers while adding a 10 MW maximum power-capacity cap (effectively banning hyperscale projects), raising the square-footage cap for 'medium' data centers to 110,000 sq ft, and requiring two weeks' advance notice to property owners within 1,000 ft of a proposed site's neighborhood meeting. County Attorney D. Berry Baxter, backed by outside zoning counsel and the Kentucky Association of Counties, concluded KRS 100.211(8)'s 90-day deadline for zoning MAP amendments does not apply to this zoning TEXT amendment, so no statutory deadline forces a vote. The Fiscal Court's public hearing and final (second-reading) vote on KOC 26-920-5 is now calendared for 2026-10-06, after this research date. The moratorium (KOC 25-910-508, extended by KOC 25-910-520 'until data center regulations are approved') has no fixed end date -- it remains the operative instrument until that vote occurs (or another statutory event ends it), consistent with an Aug. 19, 2026 news report confirming the moratorium 'remains in place' pending the Fiscal Court's next action.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23. Town Counsel Donna MacNicol told voters before the vote that the BESS portion was unlikely to survive Attorney General review because standalone BESS is treated as a protected/solar-adjacent use under G.L. c. 48, Section 3, and recommended splitting the article into two motions; voters instead approved the combined article as written (several Massachusetts towns, including Blandford, Worthington, and Wendell, had similar BESS moratoria disapproved by the AGO's Municipal Law Unit in 2026). The full County Legislature passed a 180-day moratorium on data-center and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) land-use applications by an 8-1 vote (one member excused) on 2026-06-22. Per KCTV5, the ordinance then went to County Executive Phil LeVota, who had 10 days to sign or veto; no veto was reported in subsequent coverage found in this pass, but the Executive's signature was not independently confirmed, and the exact ordinance/file number of the version that received final passage (whether an amended Ordinance 6074 or a substitute) was not confirmed from a primary Legistar record, which returned an access error to automated fetch.
trigger: Rapid emergence of data center and battery energy storage system applications; perceived gaps in the Jackson County Unified Development Code; infrastructure, environmental, public safety, and public notice concerns.
affectedProjects: Would apply to Jackson County's acceptance, processing, and approval of rezoning applications, CUPs, SUPs, site plans, and building permits for data centers or BESS facilities, per Ordinance 6074 text. The ordinance contains no project-specific exemption language. The Nebius EastGate project sits in the City of Independence, which exercises municipal zoning authority over its incorporated territory; the county-level moratorium therefore does not reach city-issued Independence approvals (confirmed from Ordinance 6074 text downloaded from Jackson County Legistar 2026-04-29).
outcome: If adopted, the county would use the pause to draft long-term code provisions and enhanced public notice requirements.

currentStatus: Replaced and lifted as of 2026-07-27. On August 18, 2026 the Board separately voted 5-0 to permanently ban data center construction/operation within Basin 162 (Pahrump Valley) -- reported as Nevada's first outright local data-center ban -- while directing staff to bring county-wide siting regulations (Bill No. 2026-14) for the remainder of the county. currentStatus: Extended via Ordinance 2026-14, adopted as an emergency measure at the 2026-07-06 Council meeting, imposing another 180-day moratorium (through approximately 2027-01-02); succeeds the original Ordinance 2025-13 (expired 2026-06-20). Active as of 2026-09-23; unaffected by the separate dispute below over the EdgeConneX development agreement. Separately, the underlying EdgeConneX development agreement (Resolution 06-2026, adopted 2026-04-06 as an emergency measure and exempted from the village's own data center moratorium) remains contested. The Ohio Supreme Court ruled 2026-08-07 (State ex rel. McNamara-Smith v. Grube) that Ashville's fiscal officer improperly refused to certify a citizen referendum petition against Resolution 06-2026 because the emergency declaration was not adequately justified; the Pickaway County Board of Elections then voted unanimously to place the referendum on the 2026-11-03 general-election ballot. Village Council subsequently introduced Resolution 16-2026 to repeal Resolution 06-2026 outright and moot the referendum; a 2026-09-08 motion to waive the second and third readings and pass it immediately fell short of the five-vote supermajority required (final tally of 4 in favor, after Mayor Clark broke an initial 3-3 tie, which the council's own rules held insufficient), and at the 2026-09-21 meeting Council instead advanced the repeal to a third reading scheduled for 2026-10-05. As of 2026-09-23, Resolution 06-2026 has not been repealed and the referendum remains scheduled for the November ballot.

outcome: Resolution 06-2026 authorized a development/consultant-funding agreement (Term Summary, Exhibit A) with EdgeConneX/PowerConneX, allocating $39,300 for GAI Consultants' independent technical review of the proposed project. It did not repeal the moratorium, which was instead independently extended by Ordinance 2026-14 on 2026-07-06. As of 2026-09-23, Resolution 06-2026 itself remains legally intact but contested: the Ohio Supreme Court ordered the village to certify a citizen referendum against it (decided 2026-08-07), the referendum is on the 2026-11-03 ballot, and a Council attempt to repeal Resolution 06-2026 and moot that vote (Resolution 16-2026) has twice failed to gather the votes needed to advance quickly and is now set for a third reading on 2026-10-05.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through Dec. 31, 2026 (the term as actually adopted, notwithstanding the ordinance's '365-day' caption -- see legal_basis) or the effective date of new data-center zoning regulations, whichever is earlier. An Aug. 24, 2026 Tulsa Flyer report confirms the moratorium 'went into effect March 25 and expires Dec. 31,' that the Planning Office's first 60-day report has been produced and recommends reclassifying data centers by square footage and widening setbacks from 250 to 1,500 feet, and that final zoning recommendations are due to Council in November 2026, after which Council could adopt them or extend the moratorium. legalBasis: Tulsa City Council File/Ordinance No. 26-196 (final substitute version "26-196-3"), reviewed by the Urban Development committee and Council on 2026-03-11 and adopted by the Budget/Special Projects committee and Council on 2026-03-25. A redlined draft of the ordinance (marked 'JCB 3/25/26') shows the bill's caption and Section 4 term were amended from a flat '365-DAY' moratorium to a fixed expiration of 'December 31, 2026, or on the effective date of an ordinance amending data center regulations..., whichever is earlier'; the amendment also renumbered sections to add a Section 4 '60-DAY REPORTS' requirement for the Planning Office. This resolves the tension between the city's caption text and Tulsa Flyer's '9 months' reporting: the final adopted term is the Dec. 31, 2026 calendar date, not a literal 365-day count from adoption.

currentStatus: Active as of the July 31, 2026 research date. Effective immediately upon adoption, the resolution bars submission, acceptance, processing, or approval of new land-use applications for new or expanded data centers or battery energy storage systems as primary uses. Applications already under review are not affected. Runs 120 days (to approximately 2026-11-24) absent extension or repeal, with council review required before expiration.
legalBasis: Resolution No. 2932, adopted by the Hillsboro City Council at a special meeting on July 27, 2026
trigger: City sought time to study data center and battery storage impacts and develop code amendments; contemporaneous coverage described Hillsboro as the first Oregon city to adopt a data center land-use moratorium
affectedProjects: New or expanded stand-alone data center or battery energy storage system land-use applications submitted after July 27, 2026; does not affect applications already under review.
outcome: Enacted moratorium on new data center and battery storage land-use applications while the city studies impacts and develops code amendments.

currentStatus: Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Board of Commissioners voted unanimously in early August 2026 to start the formal process for a countywide data center moratorium; because Oregon law requires 45 days' notice to DLCD before a public hearing, the earliest possible adoption was not before roughly mid/late September 2026, and no report of a completed final vote was found as of this pass (a September 15, 2026 article still described the county as 'considering' the moratorium). No data center land-use application had been filed in the county as of this pass. [VERIFY instrument number; adoption date; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.55 in the 2026-09 refresh]
legalBasis: Board of Commissioners motion (approx. 2026-08-04/08-05) directing staff to begin the formal 45-day notice process required under Oregon law before adopting a data center moratorium; no ordinance number exists because the moratorium itself had not been adopted as of this pass.
trigger: Commissioner Diana Helm reversed an earlier position welcoming data centers, citing conversations with people in the AI/data-center industry who recommended the county not allow them; commissioners cited a desire to act proactively (no land-use application for a new data center had been filed in the county, which has only one existing data center, operated by Siemens in Wilsonville) and cited Hillsboro's and Salem's moratoria as models.
affectedProjects: None; county officials stated no land-use application for a data center had been filed, and the only existing data center in the county is operated by Siemens on its Wilsonville campus.
outcome: Board of Commissioners voted unanimously to begin the formal process for a countywide data center moratorium; not yet adopted as of this pass.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23. Moratorium halts construction of all data centers (as a primary use) and accessory data centers with facility capacity greater than 2 megawatts, effective 2026-09-21 through 2027-01-19. City Attorney Dan Atchison based the moratorium on a compelling need to prevent public harm, citing the city's water supply risk from the impending deep drawdown of the Detroit Reservoir (serving roughly 220,000 water customers). The moratorium does not block Verrus's already-filed land use application for a 600,000-square-foot data center (filed late July 2026, before the moratorium), since Oregon law generally requires applications to be reviewed under rules in effect when filed, but the city attorney confirmed construction itself can be prohibited during the moratorium.
legalBasis: Moratorium ordinance adopted by the Salem City Council on 2026-09-21, following an August 3, 2026 council vote to move forward with the moratorium and a resolution to begin updating zoning/land-use code; required 45-day notice to the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development preceded formal adoption.
trigger: specific_project
affectedProjects: Verrus Group filed a land use application in late July 2026 for a roughly 600,000-square-foot data center in Salem; the application proceeds under pre-moratorium review rules, but the moratorium bars construction while it is in effect.
outcome: City Council unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium halting data center construction while the city develops permanent zoning and land-use regulations.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23. Moratorium prevents city planning staff from considering any new data center land-use application, effective 2026-09-14 through 2027-01-12. Adopted after the city learned that data center developer Verrus (which had separately applied to build in Salem, where its application drew significant public resistance) was exploring development of a data center on a 237-acre privately owned Southwest Industrial Reserve Area parcel brought into Woodburn's urban growth boundary in 2025; Woodburn had not received a formal application as of adoption. The city separately adopted an ordinance in June 2026 designating data centers as a conditional use in that industrial reserve area, and has hired a consultant (Thomas Consulting Group) to help review and potentially revise its development code for data centers.
legalBasis: Moratorium ordinance adopted by the Woodburn City Council on 2026-09-14; the city filed the required 45-day notice of intent to consider a moratorium with the Oregon Department of Land Conservation and Development on 2026-07-30 before the council could act.
trigger: specific_project
affectedProjects: No formal application received; city staff learned that data center developer Verrus was exploring a site 'in or near Woodburn,' including the 237-acre Southwest Industrial Reserve Area.
outcome: City Council unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium on considering new data center applications while the city reviews and potentially revises its development code.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 180-day expiry (~2027-01-09). Adopted via a unanimous June 22, 2026 motion and formalized by resolution at the July 13, 2026 meeting, the moratorium pauses applications for six business types (data centers, power generation plants, large-scale/accessory solar, last-mile fulfillment centers, micro-warehouses, dispensaries) while the township prepares a curative amendment to correct the declared invalidity. No news of an extension, adoption of the amendment, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
legalBasis: Adams Township Board of Supervisors resolution (a follow-up to the June 22, 2026 motion), invoking the municipal curative amendment process under the PA Municipalities Planning Code and declaring the zoning ordinance's exclusion of the six business types 'does not bear a substantial relationship to the public health, safety or morals' of residents, and that a sweeping ban 'cannot pass constitutional muster' and is therefore invalid (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap: current zoning ordinance does not address data centers, power generation plants, large-scale/accessory solar, last-mile fulfillment centers, micro-warehouses, or dispensaries, allowing any of them to be built anywhere in the township. Board Chairman Russell Ford emphasized the action was preemptive, not prompted by any pending application.
affectedProjects: None named; officials stated the moratorium was preemptive and not prompted by any pending application for any of the six covered business types.
outcome: Adams Township Board of Supervisors adopted a 180-day moratorium (via a June 22, 2026 motion, formalized by resolution on July 13, 2026) on six business types including data centers and large-scale solar, to allow time to draft a curative amendment to the zoning ordinance.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day curative-amendment period from 2026-06-08. No data center application was pending at adoption.
legalBasis: Township Council resolution, Municipal Curative Amendment (Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code Section 609.2)
trigger: Zoning ordinance lacked provisions for data centers, solar energy, and wind energy.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 180-day expiry (~2026-12-13/14). Adopted by unanimous Borough Council motion on 2026-06-16, pausing data center development in the borough and barring data centers from using Brookville's municipal water system (which also serves Corsica, Pinecreek Elementary School, and the Jefferson County Fairgrounds outside the borough). The action was prompted by unofficial word of two possible nearby data center projects -- one in Pine Creek Township, one in Rose Township -- that officials estimated could together require about 2.4 million gallons of water per day; no formal application had been filed for either as of adoption. No news of an extension, permanent ordinance, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
legalBasis: Confirmed via three independent contemporaneous news reports (WPSU, The Courier-Express/Jeffersonian Democrat, and explorejeffersonpa.com/EYT) that the moratorium was adopted as a Borough Council motion -- made by Second Vice-President Randy Bartley during the property committee's report at the June 16, 2026 regular meeting -- rather than as a separately numbered ordinance or resolution. The Courier-Express: 'The moratorium was approved during a report by the property committee regarding some rezoning in the borough. The motion was made by Randy Bartley... The motion passed unanimously.' No ordinance or resolution number exists for this action because it was adopted by motion.
trigger: Water-resource concerns tied to potential nearby data center projects; no formal application was pending.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23. 180-day municipal curative amendment adopted 2026-08-12, giving the township until approximately 2027-02-08 to draft and adopt data-center zoning standards; effectively functions as a moratorium on new data-center proposals during that period, per township solicitor Brian Farrington ('I don't want to call it a moratorium, but effectively, it is').
legalBasis: Buffalo Township municipal curative amendment under PA Municipalities Planning Code Section 609.2 (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed)
trigger: Regulatory gap: township zoning ordinance does not address data centers; adopted proactively -- following similar action in other Butler County townships (Adams, Center, Lancaster) -- specifically to prevent a developer from forcing the issue via a landowner curative amendment.
affectedProjects: None named; no application was pending as of adoption.
outcome: Buffalo Township Board of Supervisors created a municipal curative amendment, giving the township 180 days to draft data-center zoning rules and effectively barring new data-center proposals during that period.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-07-31; 180-day curative-amendment period from 2026-05-12.
legalBasis: Resolution No. 05122026, Municipal Curative Amendment (Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code Section 609.2)
trigger: Zoning ordinance did not define or regulate data centers.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 180-day expiry (~2026-12-07). No data center application had been filed in Center Township as of adoption; the pause was adopted proactively, alongside similar action in neighboring Adams Township, while Center, Summit, Jefferson, Penn, Lancaster, and Forward townships in Butler County all worked on data-center zoning ordinances as of the July 31, 2026 countywide roundup. No news of a permanent ordinance adoption, extension, or repeal specific to Center Township was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
legalBasis: Curative amendment approved by the Board of Supervisors on 2026-06-10, halting data center and power-generation-plant-system development for 180 days (Supervisor Phil Wulff: 'the board of supervisors needs to undertake formal action to remedy an exclusionary omission... in the zoning ordinance'). A July 31, 2026 Butler Eagle roundup of Butler County municipalities independently confirms Center Township (along with Adams Township) 'went as far as enacting 180-day moratoriums on data centers and related developments.' Specific resolution/ordinance number and official minutes were not located in sources reviewed.
trigger: No data center development request had been received; adopted proactively.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23; the moratorium's precise end date is not independently confirmed (estimated late October 2026 from a six-month term starting April 30, 2026). Since adoption, Linde Corporation's application (submitted the same day as the moratorium) proceeded through contested public hearings, including a May 7, 2026 planning commission session drawing roughly 250 attendees. On 2026-09-14, the Board of Supervisors -- following a unanimous Planning Commission recommendation to deny -- unanimously rejected Linde's preliminary land development plan for 20 data center buildings and two gas-fired power plants, finding it did not meet the township's Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (insufficient detail on environmental protections, stormwater management, and infrastructure impacts). Linde is widely expected to appeal to Wayne County Court. [VERIFY instrument number; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.65 in the 2026-09 refresh]
legalBasis: Clinton Township Board of Supervisors vote (April 30, 2026 meeting) adopting a six-month moratorium on data-center applications while a draft Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO) amendment, prepared by Solicitor Jeffrey Treat since a December 2025 request, is reviewed by the Township and Wayne County Planning Commissions (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Specific project combined with a regulatory gap: the moratorium was adopted the same day Linde Corporation submitted a proposal for a data center and gas-fired power plants on a 758-acre former mining parcel near Browndale, on land identified as containing one of only two 'exceptional value waters' streams in Wayne County (Roger's Creek, tributary to the Lackawanna/Susquehanna); the township had already been drafting data-center standards since a December 2025 board request.
affectedProjects: Linde Corporation's proposed $6 billion data center and two gas-fired power plants on 758 acres of former mining land near Browndale; the application was submitted April 30, 2026 (the same day the moratorium was adopted) and was unanimously rejected by the Board of Supervisors on 2026-09-14 for failing to meet SALDO standards; an appeal to Wayne County Court is expected.
outcome: Clinton Township (Wayne County) Board of Supervisors voted on 2026-04-30 to impose a six-month moratorium on data-center applications while it finalized a data-center ordinance; the township separately and unanimously rejected the pending Linde Corporation data center/power-plant land development plan on 2026-09-14 for failing to meet subdivision and land development standards.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its official 2027-01-03 end date (per the township's own presentation). A draft ordinance establishing a Data Center Overlay district (100-acre minimum parcel, 250-foot perimeter setback, 90-foot height cap, 50-foot landscaped buffer, acoustic standards, etc.) has been presented publicly but not yet adopted as of this research pass; residents continue to organize opposition to rezoning for data centers in the township.
legalBasis: Resolution 2026-13 (Conewago Township, York County), adopted unanimously at the July 7, 2026 Board of Supervisors meeting, invoking the municipal curative-amendment process to prevent a developer from filing a substantive validity challenge to the township's zoning ordinance over its silence on data centers.
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance did not address data centers; a draft data-center ordinance and zoning overlay map, developed with township counsel (Eckert Seamans) and engineering consultant (CS Davidson), was presented to the public at a July 23, 2026 special joint meeting of the Board of Supervisors and Planning Commission.
affectedProjects: None named; a prior 2025 proposal to rezone land near Bible Baptist Church for a data center (developer identified in some coverage) drew opposition but is treated separately from this proactive, township-wide moratorium.
outcome: Conewago Township Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted Resolution 2026-13 on 2026-07-07, a 180-day moratorium on data-center applications (ending 2027-01-03), while it develops a Data Center Overlay zoning ordinance.

currentStatus: Replaced as of 2025-09-22. The township's Aug. 11, 2025 temporary moratorium was superseded about six weeks later when supervisors voted 3-0 to permanently amend the zoning ordinance's conditional-use standards to regulate data centers, data center accessory structures, power substations, and data center campuses (covering noise, vibration, traffic and police/fire impact, and a water feasibility study requirement). The permanent amendment was later challenged by developer Brewster Land Company (landowner curative amendment / validity challenge over a 155-acre B-2-zoned parcel); the Zoning Hearing Board rejected that challenge (outcome reported as a township 'win' around 2026-05/06), and the developer has since appealed to court (as of an Aug. 31, 2026 report).
legalBasis: Dorrance Township Board of Supervisors ordinance (adopted 2025-08-11) imposing 'a temporary moratorium of the acceptance, processing, and approval of applications for data centers and similar technology, related businesses that consume large amounts of power and use water for cooling, throughout all zoning districts of the township'; superseded by a permanent zoning amendment adopted 2025-09-22 (unanimous 3-0 vote) establishing conditional-use standards for data centers, data center accessory structures, power substations, and data center campuses.
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with public pressure: zoning ordinance was silent on data centers; adopted after more than 100 residents packed a planning commission meeting following rumors that a data center was planned for the township, though officials said no proposal had been received.
affectedProjects: None named as pending at the original moratorium's adoption. The subsequent zoning-validity challenge came from Brewster Land Company over a 155-acre B-2 parcel, adjudicated separately by the Zoning Hearing Board and later appealed to court by the developer.
outcome: Dorrance Township Board of Supervisors adopted a temporary moratorium on data-center applications on 2025-08-11, which was replaced about six weeks later by a permanent zoning amendment (2025-09-22) establishing conditional-use standards for data centers, data center accessory structures, power substations, and data center campuses.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, nearing its computed 2026-12-13 end date. The vote does not itself adopt final zoning rules; it starts a 180-day period for officials and consultants to draft standards on where data centers may be located, how they are defined, and what development standards would apply. No application is pending in the township.
legalBasis: Doylestown Township Board of Supervisors resolution (adopted June 16, 2026) invoking the municipal curative amendment process, declaring the zoning ordinance's failure to identify or regulate data centers 'substantively invalid' (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed); township solicitor Peter Nelson advised the process requires adoption of a new ordinance within 180 days and bars reuse of the same curative-amendment tool for three years.
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance does not identify or regulate data centers as a permitted use; adopted proactively as part of a broader wave of Bucks County municipalities (following neighboring Falls Township's contested Amazon data center) acting to define and regulate the use before an application arrives.
affectedProjects: None; no data center application is pending in Doylestown Township.
outcome: Doylestown Township Board of Supervisors voted on June 16, 2026 to begin a 180-day municipal curative amendment process, temporarily freezing any data-center applications while the township drafts zoning rules.

currentStatus: Nearing resolution as of 2026-09-23. The 180-day curative-amendment clock started in March 2026 (per The Center Square); Green Fig withdrew its expanded 1.7-million-sq-ft application in May 2026 amid sustained opposition and signaled intent to instead pursue its earlier, previously approved 2024 plan. A resident working group helped draft the resulting 'Data Center Ordinance,' for which the Board of Supervisors set a Sept. 24, 2026 public hearing to consider adoption (one day after this research pass); the pending Sentinel/Green Fig application is not on that hearing's agenda.
legalBasis: East Whiteland Township municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code, developed with a resident working group beginning May 2026; a Sept. 24, 2026 public hearing was set to consider adoption of the resulting ordinance
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with a specific, highly contested project: developer Green Fig's proposal (later expanded to 1.7 million sq ft) for a data center on Swedesford Road, which drew sustained community opposition; the township already had an earlier, separately approved 2024 data-center plan on the same site.
affectedProjects: Green Fig/Sentinel data center proposal on Swedesford Road; the expanded 1.7-million-sq-ft version was withdrawn in May 2026, with the developer expected to instead pursue its earlier-approved 2024 plan (details of that plan not confirmed in this pass).
outcome: East Whiteland Township Board of Supervisors initiated a municipal curative amendment in March 2026 to add data-center zoning standards; a resident working group helped draft the resulting ordinance, which was scheduled for a Sept. 24, 2026 adoption hearing.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-23 end date. The curative amendment does not affect the already-approved (March 2025) Amazon Web Services data center, which remains under construction; township staff will review the existing zoning ordinance and bring proposed amendments back to the Board within 180 days, with drafts to be posted publicly and advertised before hearings.
legalBasis: Falls Township Board of Supervisors resolution (adopted July 27, 2026) declaring a portion of the zoning ordinance 'substantively invalid' as to data centers, initiating a municipal curative amendment as a 'protective measure' against substantive-validity challenges (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with sustained public opposition to the already-approved Amazon Web Services data center (a 2-million-square-foot, 10-building campus under construction at the former U.S. Steel/Keystone Trade Center site); residents demanded clearer definitions of 'data center' and infrastructure/utility standards for future proposals.
affectedProjects: None going forward; the curative amendment explicitly does not affect the already-approved and under-construction Amazon Web Services data center at the former U.S. Steel site, whose approval (March 2025) and community pushback prompted this action.
outcome: Falls Township Board of Supervisors voted July 27, 2026 to declare part of its zoning ordinance substantively invalid as to data centers, opening a 180-day curative-amendment period to draft new zoning rules.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted unanimously at an Aug. 20, 2026 special meeting; bars new data center/technical development applications for up to 180 days (through approximately 2027-02-16) while the township completes a curative amendment. Does not apply to PNK Group's pending application, which continues to be processed and has been the subject of contested public hearings (through at least Aug. 25, 2026), including reports that several formerly opposed neighboring households signed non-opposition or support letters after a confidential settlement offer from PNK.
legalBasis: Resolution 2026-03 (Gregg Township, Union County), adopted at an Aug. 20, 2026 special meeting
trigger: Curative-amendment process to add data-center zoning standards, prompted by PNK Group's pending application for a large data-center campus at Great Stream Commons and the absence of applicable standards in the township's zoning ordinance.
affectedProjects: PNK Group's pending application for a data center at Great Stream Commons (an initial 60-megawatt phase with a full build-out up to 240 megawatts) is expressly excluded from the moratorium and continues to be processed.
outcome: Gregg Township (Union County) Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution 2026-03, a moratorium on new data-center applications (excluding the pending PNK Group application), to allow time to complete a curative amendment to the zoning ordinance.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-07-31 (expires approximately 2026-12-05).
legalBasis: Municipal curative amendment adopted by the Hazle Township Board of Supervisors, temporarily invalidating portions of the township zoning ordinance for 180 days on the stated grounds that the ordinance is deficient because it does not address data centers (instrument number not located).
trigger: Followed sustained community opposition ("Project Hazelnot") to NorthPoint Development's proposed ~1,300-acre, 15-building "Project Hazelnut" data-center campus with substation, which the township had already rejected in November 2025 and which a Luzerne County judge ruled against in spring 2026.
affectedProjects: NorthPoint Development's proposed 'Project Hazelnut' data-center campus, previously denied by the township and by a county court.
outcome: Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted a 180-day curative amendment pausing consideration of new data-center applications while permanent zoning language is drafted.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-10 end date. The township now has six months from adoption to develop an ordinance amendment with help from the township solicitor and planning commission, using nearby townships' ordinances as models. No news of an extension, adoption of the amendment, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
legalBasis: Little Britain Township Board of Supervisors resolution (adopted July 14, 2026) declaring existing ordinances invalid regarding data centers and related uses because they are not addressed, initiating a municipal curative amendment (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap: the township has no ordinance specifically addressing data centers; adopted proactively while the board develops a new ordinance modeled on those of nearby townships.
affectedProjects: None named; adopted proactively rather than in response to a pending application.
outcome: Little Britain Township Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted a resolution on 2026-07-14 imposing a 180-day moratorium on data-center applications, following a preliminary June 9, 2026 vote to move forward with the concept.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its 180-day statutory ceiling (~2026-12-15). The county's Planning & Community Development Department, working with consultant Entech Engineering, introduced a full draft curative amendment (covering power sourcing, water supply, permitted zones, setbacks, noise, and decommissioning) to the County Planning Commission in September 2026; Commission Chair Jason Bogle stressed it remains a draft, and public-comment hearings before the Board of Commissioners were expected to begin around mid-November 2026, ahead of the statutory deadline. Commissioner Marc Sortman has repeatedly clarified that the county's own zoning authority covers only the 19 municipalities in its zoning partnership (which does not include Muncy Township, a separate PA MPC curative-amendment moratorium already tracked in this inventory as pa-muncy-township-2026); other municipalities must adopt their own ordinances.
legalBasis: Resolution 2026-16 (Lycoming County), adopted 3-0 by the Board of Commissioners at its regular public meeting on 2026-06-18, declaring the county's zoning ordinance (enacted 1991, amended 2021) 'substantially invalid' for failing to provide appropriate zoning regulation of data centers and accessory/similar uses, and triggering the 180-day curative-amendment period under the PA Municipalities Planning Code.
trigger: County zoning ordinance lacked appropriate regulation of data centers and related uses.

currentStatus: Superseded. The Montour County Board of Commissioners enacted Ordinance No. 1-2026 ('Data Center Land Use Ordinance') on April 14, 2026 -- before the moratorium's own nominal 2026-05-17 expiration -- amending the County Zoning Ordinance to permit Data Centers as a Conditional Use in the Industrial Zoning District, subject to detailed siting, setback/buffer-yard, noise, lighting, and 'Sensitive Receptor' protections and a Conditional Use review process. The moratorium (Resolution R-11-19-2025) is no longer the operative instrument; Ordinance 1-2026 governs data center siting in Montour County as of 2026-07-31.
legalBasis: Resolution R-11-19-2025 (the moratorium, now superseded); Ordinance No. 1-2026, the 'Data Center Land Use Ordinance,' enacted by the Montour County Board of Commissioners on April 14, 2026, amending the County Zoning Ordinance to define and regulate Data Centers and Data Center Accessory Uses.
trigger: Concern over potential data centers or similar large-scale digital/technology facilities; county needed time for Planning Commission ad-hoc committee ordinance work
affectedProjects: No pending data center applications at enactment; Talen Energy later sought rezoning of Anthony Township parcels for a data-center-related industrial use
outcome: Following the 2026-02-12 denial of Talen Energy's zoning map amendment, the county completed and enacted the Data Center Land Use Ordinance (Ordinance 1-2026) on 2026-04-14, permitting data centers by conditional use in the Industrial Zoning District rather than prohibiting them outright.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, running toward its computed 2027-01-17 end date. The borough plans to use the 180-day period to review land-use impacts and prepare new zoning regulations related to data-center development; no application is reported pending in the borough.
legalBasis: Morrisville Borough Council resolution (adopted July 21, 2026) declaring a portion of the borough's zoning ordinance invalid and initiating a municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code to shield the borough from data-center-related zoning challenges (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap, adopted in the same week as neighboring Falls Township's similar action amid broader Bucks County concern over data-center energy consumption, noise, and water usage.
affectedProjects: None named; adopted proactively.
outcome: Morrisville Borough Council adopted a resolution on 2026-07-21 declaring part of its zoning ordinance invalid and opening a 180-day curative-amendment/waiting period to draft data-center zoning regulations.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, nearing its computed 2026-11-14 end date. The township presented an ordinance work-progress update on July 15, 2026 and a preliminary draft ordinance update on Aug. 12, 2026; a public hearing for comment only (no board vote that night) was advertised for Sept. 23, 2026 at Mount Carmel Area High School. No news of an extension, adoption of the final ordinance, or repeal was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23.
legalBasis: Mount Carmel Township municipal curative amendment under the PA Municipalities Planning Code; the township's own site describes it simply as the '180 day moratorium enacted on May 18, 2026,' the end result of which will be a curative amendment to correct zoning invalidities regarding data centers (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed).
trigger: Regulatory gap combined with sustained community opposition: hundreds of residents packed public meetings (including a May 13, 2026 hearing) opposing data-center development in the township; officials say they cannot outright ban the use but are working to limit and define it through zoning.
affectedProjects: None named as pending at adoption; the moratorium responded to general community opposition and rumors of data-center interest in the township rather than a specific filed application.
outcome: Mount Carmel Township Board of Supervisors adopted a 180-day moratorium on data-center proposals on 2026-05-18 to allow time to draft a curative-amendment zoning ordinance, with a public-comment hearing on the draft ordinance held Sept. 23, 2026.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-07-31; nine-month pause from the 2026-04-28 vote runs to approximately late January 2027 unless superseded by earlier zoning adoption.
legalBasis: Board of Supervisors motion/temporary moratorium adopted at the April 28, 2026 special meeting; no separately numbered ordinance or resolution identified in the sources reviewed
trigger: Lack of existing zoning provisions addressing data centers.

currentStatus: Replaced as of 2026-08-12. Resolution No. 621 (adopted 2026-05-06) opened a 180-day curative-amendment window (statutory ceiling 2026-11-02); following an Aug. 12, 2026 public hearing, the Board of Supervisors adopted the resulting curative amendment early, creating a new H-1 (Heavy Industrial) Zoning District (carved from the southern portion of the existing M-1 Industrial District) as the only zone where data centers, data center accessory uses, and disaster recovery facilities may locate (as Conditional Uses); these uses are no longer permitted in the township's ED or M-1 districts. The Board said it will address additional concerns in a future amendment.
legalBasis: Resolution No. 621 (Smithfield Township), formally initiating the Municipalities Planning Code curative-amendment process; superseded by the curative amendment adopted 2026-08-12 establishing a new H-1 (Heavy Industrial) Zoning District for data centers, data center accessory uses, and disaster recovery facilities
trigger: Regulatory gap: zoning ordinance did not specifically address data centers; adopted proactively to develop tailored standards and a dedicated zoning district.
affectedProjects: None named; adopted proactively.
outcome: Smithfield Township Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No. 621, opening a municipal curative-amendment window that it used to adopt (on 2026-08-12, ahead of the Nov. 2, 2026 deadline) a permanent zoning amendment confining data centers to a newly created H-1 Heavy Industrial District.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23, ending 2026-11-02. Bars new data-center development but does not apply to TECfusions' existing Building J permits (already operational, delivering GPU capacity per an Aug. 27, 2026 company release) or to a land-development plan the township approved Aug. 5, 2026 for further work on that building. A new draft ordinance (H-1-style Heavy Industrial standards, noise/vibration studies, and a contested requirement that developers provide their own baseload power generation) was under Planning Commission review, with a meeting held Sept. 15, 2026. A land-use appeal (Protect PT and two New Kensington residents, filed in Westmoreland County Court of Common Pleas) argues the township improperly allowed TECfusions' expansion to proceed via permits and a land-development-plan approval without requiring a full zoning/special-exception process.
legalBasis: Upper Burrell Township municipal curative amendment/moratorium on new data-center development (specific resolution number not located in sources reviewed)
trigger: Public pressure over TECfusions' 'Keystone Connect' hyperscale data-center campus (up to 1,400 acres, potentially up to 3 gigawatts, at the former Alcoa/Arconic Technical Center); residents sought more transparency and regulation before further development.
affectedProjects: TECfusions' 'Keystone Connect' campus at the former Alcoa/Arconic Technical Center (up to 1,400 acres, potentially up to 3 GW); Building J is already operational and exempted from the moratorium, and a land-development plan for further work on that building was approved Aug. 5, 2026 despite the moratorium.

currentStatus: Active as of 2026-09-23.
